Learning Objectives
Review clavicular fracture classifications and how they pertain to management.
Discuss surrounding anatomy and how it pertains to deformity after fracture and dangers to
avoid during surgical management.
Demonstrate how to obtain a complete patient history and physical examination, with
appropriate imaging studies and knowledge of associated injuries.
List indications for nonsurgical and surgical management pertaining to the three anatomic
divisions of the clavicle (medial, middle, lateral).
Review treatment options for clavicular fractures and common pitfalls and complications after
management.

Overview
Approximately 15% of clavicular fractures are distal-third fractures, 80% are middle-third
fractures, and 5% are medial-third fractures.
Original research on clavicular fractures performed by Neer1 and Rowe2 in the 1960s
demonstrated low nonunion rates, and a culture of nonsurgical management ensued.
More recent studies suggest a higher rate of nonunion in patients with a displaced clavicle
fracture.3
Displaced clavicle fractures also result in decreased functional outcomes if they heal in a
malunited position.4

Overview
Clavicular fractures are common injuries that frequently occur in a younger patient
population but also occur in the elderly population as a result of lower-energy trauma.
The midshaft clavicle is the most common site of fractures (80%), with the incidence of
distal- and medial-third fractures being 15% and 5%, respectively. The higher incidence
of midshaft fractures is the result of thinning of the clavicle in the midsection and
because this areas is devoid of muscular and ligamentous attachments. Original
research on clavicular fractures by Neer1 and Rowe2 demonstrated incidences of
nonunion of 0.1% and 0.8%, respectively. More recent research calls these numbers into
question: a meta-analysis by Zlowodzki et al3 reported nonunion rates of 5.9% across all
clavicular fractures and 15.1% in patients with a displaced fracture. McKee et al4
retrospectively reviewed patients with a healed displaced clavicle fracture to evaluate for
strength and endurance deficits. The most considerable deficiencies were reported in
abduction endurance, which was 67% compared with that of the unaffected extremity.4
Epidemiology
Fractures of the clavicle account for 3.8% of all fractures and compose 35% to 45% of all
shoulder girdle injuries.


Epidemiology
Clavicular fractures are most common in the younger, active male population as a result
of a fall during sports activity or motor vehicle trauma. They also occur in the elderly
patient population, with a predilection for lateral clavicle fractures resulting from a fall
from a height directly onto the shoulder.5
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
Clavicle osteology (Figures 1 and 2)
The clavicle is the only long bone to ossify by intramembranous ossification and is the first to
ossify.
The width of the clavicle varies in a medial to lateral direction and is narrowest at its
midportion.
The medial and lateral aspects of the clavicle are composed of larger proportions of
cancellous bone compared with the midportion.
The inferolateral aspect of the clavicle contains the conoid tubercle and the trapezoidal ridge.
The clavicle serves as the primary stabilizer between the axial skeleton (via the
sternoclavicular joint) and the appendicular skeleton (via the acromioclavicular joint).

(Reproduced from Eichinger JK, Balog TP, Grassbaugh JA: Intramedullary fixation of clavicle
fractures: Anatomy, indications, advantages, and disadvantages. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2016;24[7]:455-464.)

Figure 2 Illustration of the acromioclavicular joint shows the surrounding anatomy of the
clavicle, including the attachments of the conoid and trapezoid (coracoclavicular ligaments)
and the connection to the acromion through the acromioclavicular ligaments. (Reproduced
from Simovitch R, Sanders B, Ozbaydar M, Lavery K, Warner JJ: Acromioclavicular joint
injuries: Diagnosis and management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2009;17[4]:207-219.)

Osteology
The clavicle is the only long bone to ossify by intramembranous ossification and is
the first to ossify, at approximately 5 weeks of gestation. Clavicular cross-sectional
anatomy varies in that it is wider at its articulations with the sternum and acromion
and narrows at its midportion. The conoid tubercle and the trapezoidal ridge are
present at the inferolateral clavicle and serve as attachment points for the conoid
and trapezoid ligaments. Because the clavicle is the sole osseous bridge between
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:41 AM
AAOS | Clavicular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000632
5/38

the axial and appendicular skeletons, it serves as the primary stabilizer between
these systems.
Vascular Anatomy
Blood supply
The primary blood supply to the clavicle is periosteal; no nutrient blood supply is present.

Vascular Anatomy
In a cadaver model dissection, Knudsen et al6 reported that the clavicle was primarily
supplied by the suprascapular, thoracoacromial, and internal thoracic arteries. The
authors further injected these arteries to find a nutrient artery penetrating the cortex
into the medullary canal but did not find such an artery. Therefore, they concluded that
the primary blood supply to the clavicle comes from a periosteal source.6
Neurologic Anatomy
The supraclavicular nerve is a superficial nerve that typically crosses the clavicle in two or three
branches.

Neurologic Anatomy
The supraclavicular nerve is commonly transected when approaching the clavicle,
leading to characteristic postoperative numbness over the proximal chest wall. Less
commonly, a painful neuroma can result from transection of this nerve. Preservation of
these sensory nerves has been proposed during the surgical approach. Nathe et al7
reported that the nerve passes over the clavicle in two to three branches, with safe
zones within 2.7 cm of the sternoclavicular joint and 1.9 cm of the acromioclavicular joint
(Figure 3). Meticulous dissection is recommended between these points if attempting to
preserve these nerve branches.

Figure 3 Illustration shows the two common patterns of supraclavicular nerve anatomy.
Two branches crossing over the clavicle (medial and lateral) are observed in
approximately one-half of the population, with the other one-half of the population
having three branches (medial, intermediate, lateral). The illustrations show the typical
location of these nerves and the proposed safe zones for each group. Group 1 (A) is for
specimens with two branches. Group 2 (B) is for specimens with three branches. CI =
confidence interval. (Reproduced with permission from Nathe T, Tseng S, Yoo B: The
anatomy of the supraclavicular nerve during surgical approach to the clavicular shaft.
Clin Orthop Relat Res 2011;469[3]:890-894.)
Joints and Ligaments

The coracoclavicular ligaments
Conoid-medial; trapezoid-lateral (Figure 4).
The coracoclavicular ligaments are the primary stabilizers to superior (vertical) translation of
the distal clavicle.
Figure 4 Three-dimensional CT reconstruction image of a right shoulder shows the broad
and more medial insertion of the conoid ligament (red) compared with the lateral trapezoid
ligament insertion (blue). (Courtesy of Andrew Boltuch, DO, Pinellas Park, FL.)

Joints and Ligaments
The conoid inserts posteromedially at a distance of 45 mm from the lateral clavicle,
and the trapezoid inserts anterolaterally at a distance of 23 mm from the lateral
clavicle. The conoid is the primary restraint to superior translation, and the trapezoid
is the primary restraint to axial translation directed toward the acromion.8
Acromioclavicular ligaments
Superior, inferior, posterior, and anterior ligaments
The superior ligament is the thickest ligament, contributing the greatest amount to joint
stability.9,10 (Figure 5).
The acromioclavicular ligaments are the primary stabilizers to horizontal translation of the
distal clavicle.

Figure 5 Coronal histologic section through the acromioclavicular joint shows the thicker
superior capsular ligament (single arrow) compared with the thinner inferior capsular ligament
(double arrow). (Reproduced with permission from Salter EG Jr, Nasca RJ, Shelley BS:
Anatomical observations on the acromioclavicular joint and supporting ligaments. Am J Sports
Med 1987;15[3]:199-206.)
The superior shoulder suspensory complex (SSSC)
The SSSC is composed of four bony landmarks—distal clavicle, acromion, coracoid process,
and glenoid neck—and the supporting ligamentous complexes of the acromioclavicular
joint and the coracoclavicular ligaments (Figure 6).

bone–soft-tissue ring. (Reproduced from Goss TP: Scapular fractures and dislocations:
Diagnosis and treatment. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1995;3[1]:22-23.)
The SSSC is a bone–soft-tissue complex that provides a stable ring from which the upper
extremity is suspended.
Musculature
The muscular envelope of the clavicle includes the platysma, pectoralis major, deltoid,
trapezius, sternocleidomastoid, and subclavius muscles (Figure 7).

a right clavicle. B, Superior view shows the muscle origins in red, insertions in blue, and
ligaments in green. C, Inferior view of a right clavicle. D, Inferior view shows the muscle origins
in red, insertions in blue, and ligaments in green. (Reproduced from Llusá M, Merí À, Ruano D:
Osteology, in Cabanela ME, Mendoza-Lattes S, Sanchez-Sotelo J, eds: Surgical Atlas of the

Musculoskeletal System. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2008, pp


Musculature
Muscular attachments to the clavicle can be subdivided into medial and lateral
structures. The medial structures attaching in superior, anterior, and inferior
orientations are the sternocleidomastoid, pectoralis major, and subclavius muscles,
respectively. The lateral muscular attachments attaching at the anterior and posterior
aspects of the clavicle are the trapezius and the deltoid. The platysma is observed
superficially, draped over the anterosuperior aspect of the clavicle.
Associated Injuries
Open fractures have a high association with closed head injury and pulmonary injury
Floating shoulder
Scapulothoracic dissociation (Figure 8) 
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:41 AM
AAOS | Clavicular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000632
12/38

Figure 8 Nonrotated AP chest radiograph shows measurement of the distance from a thoracic
spinous process to the medial border of both scapulae to determine the scapular index. The
increased lateral displacement of the right scapula greater than 1 cm, an increased scapular
index (1.43), and the presence of a widely distracted midshaft clavicle fracture are indicative of
scapulothoracic dissociation. (Reproduced from Choo AM, Schottel P, Burgess AR:
Scapulothoracic dissociation: Evaluation and management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2017;25[5]:339-347.)

Associated Injuries
Taitsman et al9 reported a 75% incidence of pulmonary injury and 65% incidence of
closed head injury in association with open clavicle fractures. A high association with rib,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:41 AM
AAOS | Clavicular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000632
13/38

scapular, and spinal fractures also exists. Floating shoulder injury involves a fracture of
the clavicle and the glenoid neck. Surgical management should be considered,
particularly for displaced fractures, because this injury involves double disruption of the
SSSC.11 Scapulothoracic dissociation involves massive traction or blunt force, causing
severe soft-tissue and neurovascular injury. Typically, a clavicular or acromioclavicular
joint separation is palpable, and a careful vascular examination should be completed in
the workup of such injury. Recent studies also show that clavicular fracture displacement
and outcomes are worse in patients in whom multiple ipsilateral rib fractures are
present.
Injury Classification
The Allman classification defines fractures of the proximal (medial), middle (midshaft), and
distal (lateral) thirds of the clavicle (Figure 9).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:41 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000632

Figure 9 Illustrated diagram shows the Allman classification of clavicular fractures, which
divides the clavicle into thirds. Group I (middle third) constitutes 69% to 85% of fractures.
Group II (distal [lateral] third) constitutes 12% to 28% of fractures. Group III (medial third)
constitutes 3% to 6% of fractures. (Reproduced from Cole PA, Gammon SR, Pedri T: Fractures
of the clavicle, scapula, and glenoid, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic
Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 894-905.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:41 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000632

Neer classified lateral-third fractures based on the integrity of the coracoclavicular ligament
complex and the involvement of the acromioclavicular joint (Figure 10).
Figure 10 Illustration shows the Neer classification of distal clavicle fractures. Type I fractures
occur lateral to the coracoclavicular ligaments but do not extend into the acromioclavicular
(AC) joint. Type II fractures are subdivided into type IIA and type IIB based on the fracture
pattern relative to the coracoclavicular ligaments. Type IIA fractures occur just medial to the
coracoclavicular ligaments, resulting in greater displacement. Type IIB fractures occur between
the conoid and trapezoid ligaments. Type III fractures involve intra-articular extension into the
AC joint without ligamentous disruption. Type IV fractures occur in skeletally immature
individuals and mimic an AC joint dislocation. Type V fractures represent an avulsion of the
coracoclavicular ligaments from the clavicle with an associated distal clavicle fracture.
(Reproduced with permission from Banerjee R, Waterman B, Padalecki J, Roberston W:
Management of distal clavicle fractures. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2011;19[7]:392-401.)
Medial-third fractures are classified according to the displacement and involvement of the
sternoclavicular joint.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:41 AM
AAOS | Clavicular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000632
16/38


Injury Classification
Allman originally classified clavicular fractures by dividing the clavicle into thirds and
describing fractures based on fracture location. Group I (middle third) fractures account
for most clavicular fractures. Neer subclassified group II (lateral third) fractures based on
the integrity of the coracoclavicular ligaments, coracoacromial joint, and physis, which
can be used to help guide treatment strategy. No formal classification exists for medial-
third fractures; however, they typically are described according to displacement, fracture
characteristics, and involvement of the sternoclavicular joint. In addition, the exact
location of midshaft clavicle fractures has been shown to be centered lateral to the
midline, which is, in most patients, at a point approximately 42% of the distance from
the lateral end to the medial end of the clavicle.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Injury—Most clavicular fractures are related to a lateral blow to the shoulder from a fall (most
common) or a direct blow to the clavicle.
A small percentage of clavicular fractures are associated with more severe injuries, including
scapulothoracic dissociation, scapular fractures, rib fractures, pneumothorax, and
neurovascular compromise.

Patient History
A thorough history should be obtained in patients with a clavicular fracture. Key portions
of a patient history include the mechanism of injury, which may help determine the
presence of associated injuries. A patient’s activity level and shoulder expectations for
strength and endurance may help tailor a treatment plan appropriately. Last, the patient
should be questioned about risk factors for decreased healing potential, such as
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:41 AM
AAOS | Clavicular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000632
17/38

smoking, and the potential for postoperative noncompliance (especially substance
abuse).
Physical Examination
The typical deformity observed in patients with a middle-third fracture is caused by a medial
fragment pulled superiorly by the sternocleidomastoid muscle, with the weight of gravity
pulling downward on the lateral fragment.
A distal neurovascular examination is important because of the proximity of the brachial
plexus and the subclavian vessels to the zone of injury.
Tenting of the skin should be evaluated carefully because it may be a sign of impending open
fracture.

Physical Examination
The sternocleidomastoid pulls the medial fragment superiorly as the combined effect of
the pectoralis major, the deltoid, and gravity force the lateral fragment inferiorly and
anteriorly. Combined with various amounts of shortening, the shoulder will appear lower
and more medialized on inspection. In addition, the shoulder often rotates and/or
translates anteriorly into a protracted position. The skin should be carefully evaluated
for impending open fractures, which are signaled by areas of skin blanching and tenting
over fracture fragments.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
The clavicle forms a unique S-shaped curve on an axial view.
The distal clavicle is flat in the anterior-posterior plane.
An AP view of the clavicle and a 20° cephalad tilt view should be obtained to define
displacement with the patient upright (Figure 11).

9/3/26, 7:41 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000632
18/38

Figure 11 AP radiographs of the clavicle of a patient with a midshaft fracture demonstrate
increased displacement with the patient in an upright position (A) compared with a supine
position (B). (Reproduced with permission from Cole PA, Gammon SR, Pedri T: Fractures of the
clavicle, scapula, and glenoid, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed
3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 894-905.
A bilateral panoramic view of both shoulders should be obtained to measure clavicular
shortening.

Radiography
To evaluate shortening, separate lines originating at the midportion of the most medial
and lateral aspects of each clavicle may be drawn on an AP radiograph that includes
both clavicles. Although this measurement has been shown to be replicable, it may
result in underestimation of shortening compared with that observed on CT scans.12 The
lateral clavicle is best visualized on a Zanca view with the x-ray beam centered on the
acromioclavicular joint in 15° of cephalic tilt. Typically, CT scans are necessary for
accurate evaluation of medial clavicle fractures.
Computed Tomography
CT is the most accurate imaging modality for determining fracture shortening and
morphology; however, CT scans are not typically obtained unless associated thoracic trauma is
present.

Computed Tomography

9/3/26, 7:41 AM

19/38

A chest CT scan is commonly ordered during trauma workup and should be used to
evaluate clavicular displacement and fracture morphology if available.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Lateral-Third Clavicle Fractures
Nonsurgical management is reserved for all nondisplaced, minimally displaced, or Neer type I,
type III, and type IV fractures.
Middle-Third Clavicle Fractures
Nonsurgical management is appropriate for nondisplaced or minimally displaced middle-third
fractures. Management includes initial immobilization, with the use of a sling being sufficient.
Improved patient satisfaction with the use of a sling compared with figure-of-8 bracing have
been demonstrated in comparative studies.
Medial-Third Clavicle Fractures
Nonsurgical management is appropriate for most medial-third clavicle fractures that are
nondisplaced or minimally displaced.

Indications
Most clavicular fractures can be successfully managed nonsurgically. The decision to
pursue nonsurgical management depends on fracture severity, associated injuries, and
patient factors. Lateral-third fractures can be managed nonsurgically in patients without
fracture displacement. The integrity of the coracoclavicular ligaments also dictates
management because a higher incidence of nonunion occurs if these ligaments are
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:41 AM
AAOS | Clavicular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000632
20/38

disrupted. Therefore, Neer type I, type III, and type IV fractures can be managed
nonsurgically via initial sling immobilization; however, acromioclavicular joint
osteoarthritis common observed on the radiographs of patients with an intra-articular
(type III) fractures. These patients may require distal clavicle excision should they
become symptomatic after the healing process (Video 1). A great deal of research has
been conducted to develop indications for the surgical management of midshaft clavicle
fractures and to determine the consequences of various amounts of clavicular malunion.
Typically, nonsurgical management is reserved for fractures with less than 2 cm of
shortening and less than 100% displacement. Simple sling immobilization is
recommended because higher degrees of malunion and increased pain scores have
been reported with figure-of-8 bracing.13 Most medial-third clavicle fractures are
managed nonsurgically, resulting in a nonunion rate of 8.3%.14
Video 1 Rudzki JR: Distal clavicle fractures & SC injuries, from McKee MD, mod: Clavicle
trauma: From midshaft fractures in contact athletes to distal clavicle fractures and
acromioclavicular joint injuries. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, New Orleans, LA, March 6-10, 2018.
Contraindications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:41 AM
AAOS | Clavicular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000632
21/38

Absolute: open or impending open injury, associated vascular injury, floating shoulder with
displacement of both fractures
Relative: bilateral clavicle fracture, polytrauma, patient requiring rapid return to function
Techniques/Procedures
0 to 4 weeks: sling immobilization as needed
4 to 6 weeks: active and active-assisted motion exercises
6 to 12 weeks: active range of motion and strengthening
Outcomes
Full return to function with minimal cosmetic deformity should be expected in patients with
uneventful healing and minimal clavicular deformity.
Overall nonunion rate is 5.9%, with the rate of nonunion increasing to 15.1% in patients with a
completely displaced fracture.3
Radiographic union is expected at 28.4 weeks in patients with a displaced fracture managed
nonsurgically.15
Surgical Management
Indications
Lateral-third clavicle fractures
Surgical management is considered for Neer type II and type V fractures (especially type IIB)
in active patients. These are associated with a higher incidence of nonunion because of
deforming forces in patients with nonfunctioning coracoclavicular ligaments (Resource 1).
Middle-third clavicle fractures
Surgical indications include open fractures or fractures with concomitant injuries to
subclavian neurovascular structures, 100% displacement, more than 20 mm of shortening,
highly comminuted fractures, and multiple upper or lower extremity fractures (polytrauma).
Medial-third clavicle fractures
Surgical management is reserved for fractures with substantial displacement or posterior
displacement into the mediastinum.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:41 AM
AAOS | Clavicular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000632
22/38


Indications
Surgical indications for clavicular fractures vary depending on fracture characteristics,
associated injuries, and patient factors.16 Specific fracture characteristics meeting the
criteria for surgical management are considered in three groups based on the location of
fracture.
Typically, lateral-third clavicle fractures managed surgically include Neer type II and type
V fractures, which involve an injury rendering the coracoclavicular ligaments torn or
functionally disabled. Without functioning coracoclavicular ligaments, the resulting
vertical instability leads to a high incidence of nonunion with nonsurgical management.
In lower-demand, elderly patients, acceptance of this nonunion risk often is acceptable
because a low percentage of lateral-third clavicle fracture nonunions may be
symptomatic.17
Middle-third fracture management has evolved because these fractures were initially
uniformly managed nonsurgically, with perceived low nonunion rates and limited
functional deficits. Over time, studies have reported higher nonunion rates and lower
satisfaction scores in patients with displaced fractures. In a 2.7-year follow-up study of
displaced midshaft fractures managed nonsurgically, Fuglesang et al18 reported a
nonunion rate of 15.3% and a 24% incidence of fair-to-poor Disabilities of the Arm,
Shoulder and Hand questionnaire scores. The authors also reported that fractures with
more than 100% displacement were associated with poorer patient-reported outcome
scores.18 Hill et al19 also reported a high association between shortening greater than 2
cm and nonunion as well as unsatisfactory results. In addition, the Canadian Orthopedic
Trauma Society15 performed a randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing nonsurgical
management and plate fixation of displaced midshaft clavicle fractures and reported
that surgical management led to improved functional outcome scores with lower rates of
nonunion and malunion. The study also reported much faster time to union in surgically
managed fractures (16.4 weeks) compared with nonsurgically managed fractures (28.4
weeks).15
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:41 AM
AAOS | Clavicular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000632
23/38

Multiple subsequent RCTs have confirmed these findings. Because of these studies,
indications for the surgical management of midshaft clavicle fractures have evolved to
focus on middle-third fractures with 100% displacement and more than 2 cm of
shortening. Medial-third fractures are the most infrequently identified clavicular
fractures, with limited research available to determine surgical indications and the
consequences of malunion or nonunion. Traditional surgical indications for fracture
management involve open fracture, substantial displacement, and segmental fracture.20
Outside of fracture characteristics, indications for the surgical management of clavicular
fractures include open fracture, impending open fracture, vascular injury, progressive
neurologic deficit, multiple ipsilateral rib fractures, floating shoulder, polytrauma, and
patients requiring a faster return to function.
Contraindications
Risk factors for poor outcomes after surgical management, including substance abuse and the
ability to follow postoperative restrictions, should be considered in the decision to proceed
with surgical fixation. Surgical treatment should not be considered in patients at high risk for
postoperative falls.
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
Careful evaluation of preoperative radiographs to determine fracture comminution and ability
to achieve relative versus absolute construct stability
Determination of associated ligament disruption
Patient Positioning
Supine with reverse Trendelenburg on radiolucent surgical table, with C-arm coming in from
the patient’s head; may facilitate plating via an anteroinferior approach.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:41 AM
AAOS | Clavicular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000632
24/38

Beach-chair or semi-sitting position, with use of a beach-chair surgical table versus a regular
surgical table (reversed with head placed at foot end); a bump may be placed under the
ipsilateral scapula, and free drill trajectory and unencumbered radiographs are confirmed
before draping.
Surgical Approach
Lateral-third clavicle fractures
Surgical fixation options include all-suture–based constructs, locking plate, and hook plate
fixation.
Consideration should be made to integrate fixation to the coracoid via anchor or subcoracoid
suture fixation.
Radiographic and clinical results of hook plate fixation re favorable; however, the fixation
constructs must be removed, requiring secondary surgery.
Middle-third clavicle fractures
Implant choices include intramedullary screw or elastic nail fixation, superior plate fixation,
anteroinferior plate fixation, and dual-plating techniques. Recent biomechanical literature
has reported that superior plating may be better for axial compression and anteroinferior
plating may be better for cantilever bending. Some RCTs have reported no difference in time
to union or the rate of hardware removal.
Medial-third clavicle fractures
Surgical procedures: open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) with plate and screws, with
sternoclavicular joint augmentation or reconstruction if the fracture is very medial and little
or no fixation to the medial clavicle can be obtained

Surgical Approach
Typically, lateral-third clavicle fractures are managed via plate fixation spanning the
fracture site, with the goal of achieving appropriate purchase in the lateral clavicle. The
lateral clavicle consists of a higher proportion of cancellous bone and may be small or
comminuted. In patients in whom lateral purchase is inadequate, a hook plate spanning
the acromioclavicular joint can be used. Typically, this plate is removed 6 months
postoperatively. Alternatively, a previously contoured plate with an expanded distal
portion and divergent locked screws integrating suture or screw fixation to the coracoid

may result in stable fixation without the need for later plate removal. Typically, middle-
third clavicle fractures are managed via plate fixation or intramedullary fixation
(Resource 2). Plate apposition can be fixated in a superior or anteroinferior position,
with advantages and disadvantages associated with each location. Superior plating is
biomechanically stronger because the superior position places the plate on the tension
side of the fracture site. Another advantage of superior plating involves less deltoid
dissection required for plate apposition. Disadvantages include shorter screws and a drill
path for screw fixation that increases the risk of damage to neurovascular structures.
Despite these differences, a meta-analysis comparing anteroinferior and superior plate
positioning reported no differences in nonunion or complication rates.21 Intramedullary
fixation with the use of screws or nails has a theoretic advantage of less hardware
prominence after fixation with less vascular supply disruption; however, such fixation
may be more appropriate for simple (noncomminuted) fractures (Resource 3). Typically,
medial-third fractures are managed via plate fixation. Plates with distal screw clusters
may be useful. The medial clavicle expands and should allow for longer screw fixation.
Extreme care must be taken when drilling in an anterior to posterior direction. If fixation
in the medial fragment is not adequate, then fixation can be extended to the sternum,
with later plate removal expected.
Postoperative Management
Sling immobilization for 7 days postoperatively, after which active motion is allowed
Strengthening at 6 weeks postoperatively
Resume contact and sports activity after fracture union, typically approximately 3 to 4 months
postoperatively

Wound breakdown with plate exposure
Careful soft-tissue handling during the procedure is combined with two-layer wound closure,
with separate muscular closure over the plate.
Prominent hardware
Anteroinferior plating may be less prominent, especially in smaller patients. Females are
much more likely to undergo hardware removal. The use of previously contoured plates

One-third tubular and 3.5-mm reconstruction plates should be avoided. Surgeons should

Nonunion
Minimize soft-tissue stripping at the fracture site. The incidence of nonunion is
approximately 1% to 5%. Underlying infection (especially Cutibacterium acnes) should be
suspected if nonunion occurs after ORIF.
Neurovascular Injury

Neurovascular Injury
Slightly increased incidence in patients who undergo superior plating. Great care must
be taken when drilling from anterior to posterior at the medial-third clavicle and when
drilling superior to inferior in the middle-third clavicle. All previously reported arterial
injuries have occurred secondary to a prominent screw in the medial two-thirds of the
clavicle and have presented in a delayed manner.22 Subperiosteal dissection is
recommended posterior to the middle third of the clavicle because the subclavian vein
may be adhered to the bone in this area. Catastrophic neurovascular injury, although
rare, primarily occurs in patients who undergo delayed surgery for the management of a
nonunion or malunion.

Malunion
Shortening malunions tend to be more symptomatic in the younger and more active
patient population. Shortening has been shown to have a considerable effect on
shoulder strength and endurance, particularly abduction endurance. Cosmesis also may
be concerning because a malunited clavicle fracture results in a shoulder that takes on a
droopy and shortened appearance, with a bump usually noted at the fracture site.
Scapular malpositioning (winging) is a predominant feature in patients with a
symptomatic clavicle malunion.

Other Complications
Lateral-Third Clavicle Fractures
Complications include acromioclavicular joint arthritis in intra-articular variants, nonunion, and
loss of fixation.
Middle-Third Clavicle Fractures
Surgical complications include iatrogenic neurovascular injury, subclavian thrombosis,
pneumothorax, injury to the supraclavicular nerves, hardware prominence, infection,
nonunion, and death.
Medial-Third Clavicle Fractures
Complications are similar to those observed in patients with a posterior sternoclavicular
dislocation.
Retrosternal and mediastinal injuries are observed, including vascular, pulmonary,
esophageal, cardiac, and neurologic injuries. Thoracic surgeon backup is essential.
Hardware migration into the mediastinum also has been reported, resulting in late
intrathoracic or vascular injury if Kirschner wires are used.
Rehabilitation
Nonsurgically managed clavicular fractures require a short period of immobilization (1 to 4
weeks), with simple Codman exercises followed by quick progression to full active-assisted and
passive range of motion. Strengthening generally begins by 6 to 10 weeks, signs of
radiographic union are observed.
Surgically managed clavicular fracture rehabilitation typically begins immediately
postoperatively with full active-assisted and passive range of motion. Strengthening begins 4
to 6 weeks postoperatively.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Scapulothoracic dissociation should be considered in patients with severe displacement if
substantial distraction of the clavicle fragments or forequarter is evident on chest radiographs
